cards.back: The field is the region around a magnet or moving charge where magnetic forces act. It is a **vector** quantity, so it has both size and direction, and its strength $B$ is measured in teslas.
cards.hint: Think about the space around a bar magnet.

cards.back: **Moving charge** produces a magnetic field. In a permanent magnet this is the motion and spin of electrons, and an electric current is also moving charge. A charge at rest produces no magnetic field.
cards.hint: Magnets and currents are the two sources in the note.

cards.front: Which way do field lines run around a bar magnet?
cards.back: Outside the magnet they run from the **north pole** to the **south pole**. Inside, they continue from south to north, so each line forms a closed loop.
cards.hint: Picture the lines leaving one end and returning at the other.

cards.front: Why can magnetic field lines never cross?
cards.back: The field has only **one direction** at each point. A crossing would mean two directions at one point, which is impossible.
cards.hint: Each line shows the direction of the field at a point.

cards.front: If you cut a bar magnet in half, can you isolate a single north pole?
cards.back: No. Each piece becomes a **smaller magnet** with its own north and south pole. Magnetic poles cannot be separated.
cards.hint: Count the poles after the cut.

cards.back: A **magnetic domain** is a tiny region inside a ferromagnetic material in which the atoms' magnetic effects all point the same way.
cards.hint: Domains are microscopic and sit inside iron or steel.

cards.front: How does a magnet attract an unmagnetized iron nail?
cards.back: 1) The nail's domains point randomly, so their effects cancel. 2) The magnet's field aligns the domains. 3) The nail gets a net field. 4) Its nearer end becomes the opposite pole, so the two attract.
cards.hint: Start with what the domains are doing before the magnet arrives.

cards.front: What is the SI unit of magnetic field strength $B$?
cards.hint: Its symbol is a single capital letter.

cards.front: Why is soft iron used for temporary magnets but steel for permanent ones?
cards.back: Soft iron magnetizes easily but **loses** most of its magnetism once the field is removed. Steel resists this, so it **keeps** much of its magnetism.
cards.hint: Compare how the domains behave after the field is removed.

cards.front: Does heating or dropping a magnet make it stronger?
cards.back: No. Heating or dropping can shake the domains out of alignment, so the magnet **weakens**.
cards.hint: What happens to aligned domains when they are shaken?

cards.back: A **permanent magnet** keeps its own magnetic field without needing an external current or magnetizing field. Its field comes from aligned electron motion and spin inside the atoms.
cards.hint: Contrast it with a magnet that needs a current to work.

cards.front: A compass sits beside a wire. What does it show when the current flows, and what happens when the current stops?
cards.back: The compass **turns** while the current flows, which shows the current produces a field. When the current stops, it returns to its old direction.
cards.hint: Think about what the compass needle responds to.
